newsitem.title: USA: Republicans retain control of Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republicans retain control of Congress.

text.p: Republicans retained control of the Senate and House of Representatives Tuesday, putting President Bill Clinton on the defensive at the start of his second term.

The Republicans won open Senate seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and Clinton's home state of Arkansas where the party grabbed Senate slot for the first time since the post-Civil War era.

According to projections by the CNN television network, Republicans lost one of thier own -- three-term Sen. Larry Pressler of South Dakota, chairman of the commerce committee, who was defeated by Democratic Representative Tim Johnson.

In the House most of the freshmen who swept to victory in the Republican takeover led by Speaker Newt Gingrich two years ago were fending off challenges. The new breakdown of the House remained in doubt but Democrats had failed to pick up the 19 seats needed to regain control, according to TV network projections.

The Republicans have not controlled both houses of Congress for consecutive sessions since before the Second World War. Two years ago marked the party's return to control of Congress for the first time in 40 years.

The new Senate lineup was expected to be little different from the current 53-47 majority held by the Republicans. There were 34 Senate seats at stake in the election and the Democrats failed to achieve a mimimum net gain of three seats they needed to win back control.

In the House the party breakdown going into Tuesday's election was 235-197, with one independent and two vacant seats. The breakdown in the House, where all 435 seats were up for election, was likely to remain in doubt for some time although TV networks were projecting the Republicans had retained their majority.
While neither Republican margin would be big enough to pass the party's major agenda, it certainly could resist programmes sent to Congress by Clinton, who easily won a second term.

In the Arkansas Senate race, Republican Tim Hutchinson defeated Democrat Winston Bryant for the open seat held by retiring Sen. David Pryor to become the first Republican senator to be elected from that state since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

In Alabama Republican Jeff Sessions defeated Democrat Roger Bedford for the seat held by retiring Democrat Howell Heflin and in Nebraska Republican Chuck Hagel beat Democratic Gov. Ben Nelson for the seat of retiring Democrat James Exon.
In New Hampshire, television networks had reported that Democrat Dick Swett had defeated Republican Sen Robert Smith. But the call was premature and the result was undecided.

Democrats won hard-fought races to retain seats in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Georgia and Illinois. Republicans kept two open seats in Kansas, vacated by presidential candidate Bob Dole and Sen. Nancy Kassebaum. They also held onto Senate seats in North and South Carolina, Tennessee, Maine, Oklahoma and Mississippi.

Voters re-elected two of the Senate's most prominent conservatives -- Jesse Helms of North Carolina and 93-year-old Strom Thurmond of South Carolina who aims to celebrate his 100th birthday as a senator in six years.

Thurmond, who will be 94 on Dec. 5, fended off a challenge by Democrat Elliott Close, to head into his eighth six-year term. Helms defeated the black former mayor of Charlotte, Harvey Gantt, in a replay of their contest six years ago.
Their race was the most expensive among the Senate contests, according to the watchdog group Common Cause. Helms spent more than $19 million and Gantt more than $6 million.

In New Jersey Democratic Representative Robert Torricelli defeated conservative Republican Dick Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by Democrat Bill Bradley. The race had been marked by furious mudslinging ads from both sides.

In Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry won a third term in a high-profile race with popular Gov. William Weld. In Illinois Representative Richard Durbin defeated Republican Al Salvi, winning the open seat vacated by Democrat Paul Simon.
In Georgia triple amputee Max Cleland, former head of the Veterans Administration, held the Senate seat vacated by fellow Democrat Sam Nunn, defeating Republican Guy Millner.
